title: Mongolia's monasteries
hookLine: monasteries were torn down and monks killed; years later, practice returned

cards: On the open grasslands of Mongolia, in some places only foundations show in the grass: a line of stones, a raised floor, a scatter of broken tile. Herders ride past them.

Some of those stones were once monasteries, with chanting halls and young monks learning their texts. How does a monastery disappear? And how, years later, does practice come back to a place that had almost forgotten it?

teach.b: Buddhism had long been woven into Mongolian life, in the Tibetan form of the tradition, with monasteries large and small across the country.

Then, under a communist government closely tied to the Soviet Union, a campaign turned against it. Monasteries were torn down or emptied. Monks were arrested and killed, or forced to return to lay life and marry.
Statues were melted; texts were burned. Yet some things were hidden.

Families buried images in the ground or kept a text at the back of a chest. Some former monks kept the chants in their heads, saying them quietly at home. When the government changed, the doors opened again.

Old monks who still remembered the ceremonies taught young ones. Monasteries were rebuilt, sometimes on the old foundations, and people came back to make offerings and ask for blessings. The return wasn't neat.
Teachers had to be found, texts recovered, a whole way of training started again almost from memory. But it happened. The Dhammapada has a pair of verses for those quiet years.
Someone who recites a great deal of the teaching but doesn't live it is like a cowherd counting other people's cows.
Someone who recites only a little, but lives it, letting go of greed, hatred and delusion, has a real share in the renunciant's life.
An old monk in a back room, saying a few remembered lines under his breath, was not counting anyone's cows.
A little, kept and lived, was enough to start again.

how: Mongolian Buddhists visit rebuilt monasteries to make offerings, light butter lamps and ask monks for blessings, and some families still keep images and texts their relatives once hid.

games.q: you are a former monk. the monasteries are gone and chanting is dangerous. what do you do with the chants you know?
o: keep them quietly at home, in memory
write them on the monastery walls
games.why: some former monks kept the chants in their heads and said them quietly at home, so there was something to return.

practice: Rest your attention on the breath at the belly, and when the mind wanders off, to a plan, a worry, a song, notice it: that moment of noticing is a small return, the same shape as a chant remembered after long silence.
Say silently, back, and begin again with the next breath. Don't count the returns or judge them; let each one be welcome.

wordCard.voice: Mongolia's monasteries. Torn down in a campaign against religion, remembered in hidden texts and quiet chants, and rebuilt when the doors opened again. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali vihāra: a dwelling place for monks, the word behind 'monastery' in Buddhist texts.

carryVoice: Your line: it returned. Buried images, remembered chants, and doors that opened again. Until tomorrow.
